newsitem.title: USA: Clinton barnstorms across Lone Star State.
newsitem.headline: Clinton barnstorms across Lone Star State.

text.p: President Bill Clinton barnstormed across Texas on Friday looking to take away from Republican Bob Dole a vote-rich state that has not gone for a Democratic presidential candidate in 20 years.

On a gray day in east Texas, Clinton told a campaign rally in Longview that his economic policies were paying dividends for the American people, citing a Census Bureau report Thursday that said 1.6 million fewer people were living in poverty in 1995 than in 1994 and household income was rising.

"We can win in the state of Texas because we've done a good job for the people of Texas," Clinton told a crowd of several thousand. He was to address rallies later in the day in Fort Worth and Houston and spend the evening in Houston raising $1 million for the Democratic Party.

A Democratic presidential candidate has not carried Texas since Jimmy Carter in 1976. The state's 32 electoral votes are the third-largest prize, behind California's 54 and New York's 33, in the race for 270 electoral votes and victory.

Texas is the adopted home state of former President George Bush, the Republican whom Clinton defeated in 1992, and Bush's son is governor. Clinton lost Texas to Bush in 1992 with Texas billionaire and third-party candidate Ross Perot third.
A University of Texas poll on Sept. 19 put Clinton and Dole in a dead heat in the state, each with 41 percent support. But Republicans dismiss it.
"I don't believe it's even in Texas," Gov. George W. Bush said last week. "I don't hear that in my travels. Senator Dole will carry the state of Texas."

Clinton, his Southern accent deepening, told the Longview rally he wanted to continue working to reduce the federal budget deficit and said Dole's proposed across-the-board 15 percent tax cut would make the deficit go back up, as it did after Ronald Reagan's tax cuts.
"We don't need a U-turn. We need to bear down and go right on into the future and I want to ask you to help us," he said.

By coming to Texas, Clinton was making a strategic move, hoping to force Dole to spend time and money in the state. Political sources say Dole bought no advertising time on Texas television stations last week, an indication that he believes the state will remain Republican.
Doug Sosnik, White House director of political affairs, sounded a confident note, saying he did not see how Dole could get to 270 electoral votes without Texas.

"I think it would be hard for him. I'm not sure how easy it's going to be for him to hit 270. We are having a hard time figuring out what map, which states he's going after to get to 270. If he doesn't win Texas, I think it will be much harder," Sosnik told reporters.

Clinton's visit was a boost for the Democratic candidate for the Senate, Victor Morales, a high school teacher who came out of nowhere to win the Democratic primary by driving a pickup truck around the state in his campaign. His seeks to unseat incumbent Republican Sen. Phil Gramm but he is far behind in the polls and most analysts give him little chance of derailing the high-spending Gramm campaign.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton considered "inappropriate" remarks Morales made recently about Republican Representative Henry Bonilla but welcomed Morales' statement of regret.
Morales had called the Hispanic-American Bonilla "a wannabe white." "Where I grew up we called them coconuts, white on the inside, brown on the outside," Morales said.
"The president believes Victor Morales shares his sentiment that campaigns based on issues and not insults are the best way to make an appeal to the voters," McCurry told reporters.
Clinton was on the first day of a two-day campaign swing. He is to travel to Rhode Island and Massachusetts on Saturday.
